title: Case study: notification service
summary: Multi-channel delivery (push, SMS, email, in-app): requirements and estimation, API and data model, priority lanes, provider failover with circuit breakers, retries that respect cost, dedupe and preferences, delivery receipts and the audit trail.

units.title: Guided design: requirements, estimation, API, data model, high-level design
Deep dives: provider failover and retries; dedupe, preferences, rate limits and priority lanes

labs.title: Notification dispatcher: dedupe, priority lanes, preferences and frequency caps, provider failover with circuit breakers, bounded retries, dead letters

outcomes.text: Scope a notification service in six minutes: the clarifying questions whose answers change the design (categories, channels, triggers, preferences, delivery semantics, tenancy, retention) and non-functional requirements with numbers.

Estimate notification volume (average, peak, a campaign spike), provider throughput limits, queue backlog and drain time with Little's law, and delivery-log storage with retention and replication, and tie each number to a decision.

Design the API (idempotent create, dedupe and collapse keys, TTL, status, campaigns, preferences, provider receipt webhooks) and a data model whose partition keys follow the access patterns, with an append-only attempt log.
Draw the high-level design with the urgent and campaign paths and the receipt path traced, and justify every box by a requirement or a number.

Design provider failover: per-provider circuit breakers, timeouts as unknown outcomes, bounded retries with backoff and jitter, retry budgets, and a per-category decision on whether a duplicate or a miss is worse.

Distinguish idempotency keys, dedupe keys, collapse keys and frequency caps; evaluate preferences and quiet hours at send time; isolate priority lanes and tenants so an OTP is never behind a campaign.

Implement the dispatcher (labs/c7/dispatch): dedupe under concurrent duplicates, priority lanes, opt-out, quiet hours, a token-bucket frequency cap, provider failover with breakers, bounded retries and a dead-letter list, passing under -race.
Explain what 'delivered' means per channel, how provider receipts and webhooks update the delivery log, and which metrics and alerts tell you the service is failing before users do.
Design templates, localisation and open/click tracking without leaking PII into logs, and reason about what tracking numbers actually measure.
